title: The Lamiyya of Ibn al-Wardi
intro: This poem is attributed to Ibn al-Wardi, who died in 749 AH (1349 CE), but it was not in his diwan; it was added to the printed edition under the heading “also attributed to him, and famous among the learned and the common people, though not found in his diwan”. It is called the Lamiyya, “the poem in lam”, after its rhyme, and a manuscript in Vienna titles it Ibn al-Wardi's Counsel; it speaks to a “son”, as advice poems do: “My son, hear counsels gathered here”. It opens by renouncing love poetry and the memory of youth, commands the fear of God and recalls the nations that perished; then come the counsels: to seek knowledge, law and grammar; to write poetry but never sell it; to be content with the livelihood God allots; to give up boasting of lineage; to keep between meanness and waste; to overlook others' faults; to keep clear of rulers and of the office of judge; to keep hope short; and to travel. He then answers those who fault his verse, complains of an age that honours only the rich, and closes with a blessing on the Prophet. Its wisdom is plain and easy to remember, and some of its half-lines have passed into proverb, such as “whoever keeps to the road arrives”.

translation: Leave off the talk of songs and love poetry,
speak the decisive word, and keep away from those who jest.
1.sharh: Odes traditionally opened with love poetry; this one opens by renouncing it, and makes that the first of its counsels.

translation: Let go the memory of the days of youth:
the star of the days of youth has set.
2.sharh: Youth is a star that has gone down and will not rise again; longing for it brings nothing back.

translation: The happiest life I ever spent:
its pleasures are gone, and the sin has stayed.
3.sharh: Pleasure passes and its sin remains. This is the reason for turning from the songs and loves of youth.

translation: Leave the young beauty, pay her no heed,
and you will live in lofty honour, and be revered.
4.sharh: Chasing women brings a man low; turning from them raises him in honour.

translation: Put out of mind the instruments of pleasure that stir delight,
and the beardless youth with swaying hips.
5.sharh: The two lures of the pleasure-seeker's evenings, music and the company of handsome boys, are dismissed together.

translation: Think on the end of the beauty of the one
you love, and you will find a grievous thing.
6.sharh: Beauty fades with age and ends in the grave; to think of its end is the cure for infatuation.

translation: Fear God: the fear of God
never dwelt in a man's heart but he arrived.
7.sharh: The fear of God is a neighbour who settles in the heart. “He arrived” names no goal, so it means every goal worth reaching.

translation: Shun wine, if you are a man,
for how should one with a mind seek madness?
8.sharh: Drunkenness is madness chosen freely, and no one with his wits about him chooses madness.

translation: The man who waylays travellers is no hero:
the hero is the one who fears God.
9.sharh: Highway robbers were the strongmen of the road. True heroism, says the poet, is mastery of oneself.

translation: Believe the Law, and put no trust in
a man who watches Saturn in the night.
10.sharh: Astrologers claimed to read the future in the planets; revelation, not the stars, tells what is hidden.

translation: Thought is bewildered by the wisdom of the One
who has guided us in our ways, Mighty and Majestic.
11.sharh: “He has guided us in our ways” is the Quran's phrase (14:12). If thought cannot fathom God's wisdom, the stargazer of the line before cannot read His decree.

translation: Death is written for all creation: how many
hosts it has broken, how many dynasties ended.
12.sharh: Death is the conqueror of conquerors, and the roll call of the dead that follows bears it out.

translation: Where is Nimrod, where Canaan, and he
who ruled the earth, appointed and dismissed?
13.sharh: The question “where are they?” is an old refrain of Arabic poems of warning; the answer is always the grave.

translation: Where is Ad, where Pharaoh, and he
who raised the Pyramids? Whoever hears, imagines.
14.sharh: The line ends on a proverb: whoever hears the story of these mighty ones will draw his own conclusions.

translation: Where are those who ruled, who raised high and built?
All perished, and their towers availed them nothing.
15.sharh: Sadu and shadu, “ruled” and “raised high”, differ only in the dots of one letter. No height of rank or wall kept death out.

translation: Where are the masters of reason, the people of understanding?
Where are the learned, and the peoples of old?
16.sharh: After the kings, the wise: reason and learning save no one from death any more than power does.

translation: God will bring back every one of them
and repay each doer for what he did.
17.sharh: Death is not the end of the story: the kings and sages will all rise to be judged. The meditation on the dead ends here.

translation: My son, hear counsels gathered here,
wisdom granted to the best of faiths.
18.sharh: From here the poem is counsel, spoken to a “son” as Arabic advice often is. The best of faiths is Islam.

translation: Seek knowledge, and do not be idle: how far
good things lie from the idle.
19.sharh: The first counsel after the address is to seek knowledge. Good things are far off, and only effort covers the distance.

translation: Forsake sleep and win knowledge, for whoever
knows the worth of what he seeks thinks little of what he spends.
20.sharh: Knowledge is bought with sleepless nights, and whoever knows its worth finds the price small.

translation: Give your whole care to understanding the faith, and do not
be drawn from it by wealth and retinue.
21.sharh: A hadith says that when God wishes good for someone, He gives him understanding of the religion.

translation: Do not say its masters are gone:
whoever keeps to the road arrives.
22.sharh: The great scholars of the past are no excuse for giving up. The second half has become a proverb in Arabic.

translation: In growing in knowledge lies the humbling of your foes,
and the beauty of knowledge is doing what is right.
23.sharh: Knowledge confounds the envious, but knowledge not put into practice has no beauty.

translation: Adorn your speech with grammar: whoever
is denied the case endings in his speech is muddled.
24.sharh: A wrong ending changes the meaning, not only the sound, so speech without grammar falls into confusion, like a mind disordered.

translation: Compose poetry, and keep to my way
in casting off rewards: the world is worth less.
25.sharh: Poets lived by praising patrons for gifts; he would have his son write poetry and refuse the gifts, since the world is not worth selling verse for.

translation: It is the mark of merit, and how
fine is poetry when it is not cheapened.
26.sharh: Poetry shows a man's worth as the title on a letter shows what it holds, unless he cheapens it by selling it.

translation: The men of merit are dead; none remain
but the base-born, or those who lean on their lineage.
27.sharh: With the worthy gone, there is no one left whom a poet could honestly praise.

translation: I would not choose to kiss a hand
whose cutting off is finer than those kisses.
28.sharh: Kissing a patron's hand was the courtier's homage; he would rather see such a hand cut off.

translation: If it rewards my praise, I become
its slave; and if not, the shame is enough for me.
29.sharh: Either way he loses: a gift makes him the giver's slave, and a refusal leaves him ashamed. Better not to ask at all.

translation: The sweetest word is my saying to you, “Take”,
and the bitterest my uttering “Perhaps”.
30.sharh: To say “take” is to give; to say “perhaps” is to put off someone who asks. Some read “perhaps” as the poet's own hoping for a gift.

translation: A crust of bread spares you the kingdom of Chosroes,
and a trickle of water will serve for the sea.
31.sharh: Kisra, Chosroes, and kisra, a crust of bread, are almost the same word: contentment makes the crust equal to the empire.

translation: Consider “We have apportioned among them”:
you will find it true; in truth it came down.
32.sharh: Two Quranic phrases: “We have apportioned among them their livelihood in this world” (43:32) and “in truth it came down” (17:105). Livelihood is allotted by God, so there is no need to grovel for it.

translation: What a man gains is not won by his resolve,
no, nor is what escapes him lost through idleness.
33.sharh: He means livelihood, not knowledge: wealth comes as God allots it, whatever one's effort, whereas knowledge, as he said, is won by labour.

translation: Cast the world aside: it is one of its habits
to bring down the high and raise up the low.
34.sharh: The world is fickle, humbling the great and exalting the base, and deserves no attachment.

translation: The life of the man who does not care to gain it
is the life of the man who toils for it; no, the toiler's is more abject.
35.sharh: The man who does not chase the world lives as well as the one who wears himself out for it, and the chaser is the more abased for all he has stooped to.

translation: How many a fool is rich, with plenty,
and how many a sage has died of its ills.
36.sharh: The world does not reward wisdom: fools grow rich, and sages die poor and sick.

translation: How many a brave man never won his wishes in it,
and a coward reached the furthest of his hopes.
37.sharh: Nor does it reward courage: the pairs of fool and sage, coward and brave man show its gifts falling at random.

translation: So leave off scheming in it, and go gently:
the only scheme is to give up schemes.
38.sharh: Hila, “stratagem”, returns in the plural to make a paradox: the cleverest plan is to stop planning and trust God.

translation: Any hand that does not give of what it gains,
may God strike it with palsy for it.
39.sharh: A hand that keeps all it gets deserves to wither: the curse is the poet's scorn for meanness.

translation: Never say “my root and my branch”:
a man's root is what he has achieved.
40.sharh: Asl and fasl, “root and branch”, is the stock phrase of the man who boasts of his pedigree. What counts is what a man achieves himself.

translation: A man may rise to lead with no father behind him,
and good smelting can purge the dross.
41.sharh: A good furnace purifies the metal, and effort makes a noble man of one with no lineage.

translation: So too the rose comes from the thorn, and
the narcissus grows only from a bulb.
42.sharh: Beauty can spring from a humble root: what matters is the flower, not the stock.

translation: Yet I praise God for
my lineage, since it reaches back to Abu Bakr.
43.sharh: Having dismissed pedigree, he gives thanks for his own: gratitude for a gift, not a boast.

translation: A man's worth is what he does well,
whether he has much of it or little.
44.sharh: The saying “every man's worth is what he does well” is attributed to Ali ibn Abi Talib; the poet adds that the amount does not matter.

translation: Keep both things hidden, poverty and wealth;
earn the copper coin, and call the idler to account.
45.sharh: Hide poverty, lest you be humbled, and wealth, lest you be envied. Earn even the smallest coin, and do not indulge the idle.

translation: Put on earnestness and toil as armour, and avoid
the company of fools and of the unsound.
46.sharh: Hard work is a coat of mail that protects its wearer, and fools are company that rubs off.

translation: Between squandering and meanness there is a middle station,
for either of the two, if it lasts, will kill.
47.sharh: The middle way of the Quran (25:67): “those who, when they spend, are neither wasteful nor mean, but keep a just mean between the two”.

translation: Do not plunge into reviling lords who have passed:
they are not men to be charged with error.
48.sharh: Most likely he means the Prophet's Companions, of whom the Prophet said: “Do not revile my Companions.”

translation: Pretend not to notice some things, for
none wins praise but one who overlooks.
49.sharh: Overlooking others' faults, knowing them all the while, is what earns their praise.

translation: No man is free of an enemy, even if
he seeks solitude on a mountain top.
50.sharh: Enmity finds a man wherever he goes, so he should not hope to please everyone.

translation: Turn aside from the talebearer and shun him:
none brings a hurtful word home but the one who carries it.
51.sharh: An insult would never have hurt had no one passed it on: the talebearer is the real offender.

translation: Bear with a bad neighbour patiently, and if
you find no patience, how sweet is moving away.
52.sharh: Patience first, and if that fails, move house: nothing is sweeter than escaping a bad neighbour.

translation: Keep clear of the ruler and beware his violence:
do not defy one who, when he speaks, acts.
53.sharh: A ruler's word is a deed: his threats are carried out, so the wise keep their distance.

translation: Do not take office as judge, even if they ask you
out of desire for you; and ignore whoever blames you.
54.sharh: If the poem is his, the lines that follow speak from experience: Ibn al-Wardi was himself a judge, at Manbij.

translation: Half the people are enemies to whoever
takes charge of judgements, and that is if he is just.
55.sharh: Every judgement makes an enemy of the losing side, so even a just judge has half the people against him; an unjust one has them all.

translation: He is like a prisoner, cut off from his pleasures,
and on the Day of Gathering both his hands are chained.
56.sharh: A judge cannot enjoy what others do without falling under suspicion, and a hadith says that every man in authority will be brought on the Day of Judgement in chains, until his justice frees him or his injustice destroys him.

translation: In the deficiency and the heaviness
of the word qadi there is a lesson and an example.
57.sharh: A grammarian's joke: the judge's very name carries the deficiency and the heaviness that grammar finds in it.

translation: The pleasure of power does not equal
what a man tastes when he is dismissed.
58.sharh: The sweetness of office is less than the bitterness of losing it. Al-Ma'arri said the same of life: the grief of dying is many times the joy of being born.

translation: Offices, however sweet to the one
who tastes them, hide poison in that honey.
59.sharh: Office is poisoned honey: sweet to the taste, deadly in the end.

translation: The toil of office has worn out my body,
and my weariness comes from humouring the base.
60.sharh: Nasab, “toil”, and mansib, “office”, share a root, as if the office were named for its toil. If the poem is his, he speaks of his own years as a judge.

translation: Cut short your hopes in this world, and you will prosper:
the sign of sense is a short hope.
61.sharh: Long hope is the illusion of having all the time in the world; the wise expect death at any hour.

translation: Whoever is pursued by death,
and caught off guard, has every reason to fear.
62.sharh: Death hunts every man and may take him unawares: reason enough to keep hope short.

translation: Stay away, and visit now and then: you will be loved the more; whoever
comes and goes too often is worn down by weariness.
63.sharh: From the hadith “Visit now and then, and you will be loved the more”. Too many visits tire the host, and the visitor's welcome wears thin.

translation: Judge a sword by its edge and leave its scabbard aside;
judge a man by his worth, not his robes.
64.sharh: A sword is worth its blade, not its sheath, however finely worked; a man is worth his merit, not his clothes.

translation: Poverty does not harm merit, just as
the closing in of dusk does not harm the sun.
65.sharh: The sun is no less bright for being hidden at sunset, nor a good man less good for being poor.

translation: Your love of homelands is plain weakness:
go abroad, and you will find a substitute for your kin.
66.sharh: The thought echoes lines attributed to al-Shafi'i: “Travel, and you will find a substitute for those you leave.”

translation: Water that stays still turns stale,
and it is by its night journey that the moon grows full.
67.sharh: The moon becomes full only by travelling through its stations night after night. The same lines use the image of standing water: “I have seen that standing water spoils.”

translation: You who find fault with my words for nothing:
the rose's scent is a torment to the dung beetle.
68.sharh: Only a corrupt taste finds fault with good verse, as only the dung beetle is sickened by roses.

translation: Turn away from the arrows of my words, and take cover,
lest an arrow from Thu'al strike you.
69.sharh: His satire, like the arrows of the famous archers of Thu'al, does not miss: a warning to his critic.

translation: Do not be deceived by a man's softness:
serpents too are soft, and are shunned.
70.sharh: He warns his critic not to mistake his gentleness for weakness: snakes are soft to the touch, and still people keep away from them.

translation: I am like water, smooth and easy to swallow,
but when it is heated, it scalds and kills.
71.sharh: Water is gentle until it is heated; so is he, until he is provoked.

translation: I am like the cane, hard to break,
and yet supple: it bends whichever way you wish.
72.sharh: Cane bends every way and does not snap: yielding in manner, unbreakable in substance.

translation: Yet I live in an age when whoever
has wealth is the most exalted lord,
73.sharh: For all his virtues, he lives in an age that honours money, not learning or letters.

translation: whom all mankind must honour,
while the man of little wealth is thought of little worth.
74.sharh: Little wealth means little worth: the play on qalil, “little”, and yustaqall, “thought little of”, makes the point.

translation: All the people of this age are untried fools, and I
am one of them; so spare the itemising of the sum.
75.sharh: The total being plain, there is no need to itemise. He counts himself among the fools, which takes the sting out of the charge.

translation: And may the blessing of God my Lord, as often as
the sun rises by day and sets,
76.sharh: The poem closes, as many didactic poems do, with a blessing on the Prophet, renewed every sunrise and sunset, that is, for ever. The sentence runs on into the next line.

translation: be upon the one of Hashim who won the heights,
Ahmad the Chosen, who surpassed those of old,
77.sharh: The blessing is for the Prophet, the glory of his clan, who surpassed all who came before him.

translation: and upon his family and Companions, lords
among whom there is no weakling, only heroes.
78.sharh: “No weakling among them but a hero” is praise dressed as an exception, a figure Arabic rhetoric prizes: there is no weakling among them at all. Heroism takes the poem back to line 9: the hero is the one who fears God.

1.1.3.head: أُغنِيَّة
1.1.3.meaning: Aghani: songs. One manuscript and al-Shirwani have ghawani, “beautiful women”.

1.2.2.meaning: Al-fasl: the decisive word, which separates truth from falsehood; the Quran calls itself qawl fasl (86:13).

4.1.2.head: غادَة
4.1.2.meaning: Ghada: a young woman, soft and graceful.

5.1.1.head: اِلهَ
5.1.1.meaning: Ilha 'an: put out of mind; the verb shares its root with lahw, “amusement”, so he is told to be distracted from distraction.

6.2.5.meaning: Jalal: great; one of the Arabic words with opposite meanings, it can also mean trivial.

8.1.5.head: فَتى
8.1.5.meaning: Fata: a young man, and one with the virtues of manhood.

10.2.5.meaning: Zuhal: Saturn, which astrologers held the greatest ill omen among the planets.

13.1.2.meaning: Numrud: Nimrod, king of Babylon, whom the commentators make the king who disputed with Abraham about his Lord (Quran 2:258).

13.1.3.head: كَنعان
13.1.3.meaning: Kan'an: Canaan, son of Ham son of Noah, ancestor of the Canaanites.

14.1.2.head: عاد
14.1.2.meaning: Ad: an ancient people of Arabia, to whom God sent the prophet Hud.

14.1.4.head: فِرعَون
14.1.4.meaning: Fir'awn: Pharaoh, the Pharaoh of Moses.

14.2.3-5.meaning: Man yasma' yakhal: a proverb, “whoever hears, imagines”: hearing about others puts notions in one's mind.

15.2.5.head: قُلَّة
15.2.5.meaning: Qulal: peaks, the tops of mountains and of towers.

18.1.2.head: بُنَيّ
18.1.2.meaning: Bunayya: “my little son”, the tender diminutive.

21.1.2.head: الفِقه
21.1.2.meaning: Fiqh: understanding; the knowledge of the faith and its law.

23.1.4.head: إِرغام
23.1.4.meaning: Irgham: humbling; literally, rubbing someone's nose in the dust (ragham).

24.2.2.meaning: I'rab: the case endings of Arabic words, which show their place in the sentence.

25.2.3.meaning: Rifd: a gift, the reward a patron gave a poet.

26.1.2.meaning: Unwan: the title written on the outside of a letter, which tells what is inside; hence any sign.

27.2.1.head: مُقرِف
27.2.1.meaning: Muqrif: of base or mixed descent; properly a horse whose sire is of lesser breed than its dam.

30.2.4.head: لَعَلَّ
30.2.4.meaning: La'alla: “perhaps”, the word of hoping and of putting off.

31.1.2.meaning: Kisra: Chosroes, title of the Persian kings.

39.1.4.head: أَفادَ
39.1.4.meaning: Tufid: afada means both “to give” and “to gain”; here “give”, and in the second tufid “gain”.

41.2.2.meaning: Sabk: smelting, melting metal to purify it.

41.2.5.meaning: Zaghal: dross, base metal mixed into gold or silver.

42.2.5.meaning: Basal: onion; also the bulb from which a narcissus grows.

43.2.3-4.meaning: Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, the first caliph.

46.1.1.head: اِدَّرِع
46.1.1.meaning: Iddara'a: to put on a coat of mail.

48.1.2.head: خاضَ
48.1.2.meaning: Takhud: wade in; to plunge into talk without care.

49.1.1.head: تَغافَلَ
49.1.1.meaning: Taghafala: to feign not to notice what one has noticed.

51.1.3.meaning: Nammam: a talebearer, who carries words between people to set them against each other.

54.1.3.meaning: Al-hukm: here, the office of judge.

56.2.5.head: غُلَّ
56.2.5.meaning: Tughall: are chained; the ghull is an iron collar binding the neck and hands.

57.1.2-3.meaning: Al-naqs wa-l-istithqal: in grammar, qadi is a “defective” (manqus) noun, whose -u and -i endings are dropped as “too heavy” (istithqal) on its final ya.

62.2.1.head: غِرَّة
62.2.1.meaning: Ghirra: heedlessness, being caught off guard.

63.1.3.head: غِبّ
63.1.3.meaning: Ghibb: every other day; properly, camels watering one day and not the next.

65.2.5.meaning: Tafal: the reddening of the sky as the sun goes down.

68.2.5.head: الجُعَل
68.2.5.meaning: Ju'al: the dung beetle, said to be sickened by the scent of roses.

69.2.5.meaning: Thu'al: a clan of Tayyi', famed as archers; Imru' al-Qays wrote of “many an archer of the Banu Thu'al”.

72.1.2.head: خَيزور
72.1.2.meaning: Khayzur: cane, the khayzuran, pliant and hard to break. The editions have khayruz.

77.1.5.head: هاشِم
77.1.5.meaning: Hashim ibn Abd Manaf, the Prophet's great-grandfather, after whom his clan, the Banu Hashim, is named.

77.2.1.head: أَحمَد
77.2.1.meaning: Ahmad: one of the Prophet's names.
